newsitem.title: FRANCE: Kohl, Chirac start summit to rescue EMU pact.
newsitem.headline: Kohl, Chirac start summit to rescue EMU pact.

text.p: The leaders of France and Germany met on Friday to seek an agreement on European Union policy coordination for growth and jobs aimed at keeping the planned euro single currency on track for January 1, 1999.

German Chancellor Helmut Kohl met French President Jacques Chirac at a high-tech theme park outside this western French city and was due to meet Prime Minister Lionel Jospin separately later on Friday to seek a formula to enable France's new left-wing government to accept a pact limiting budget deficits.

The Jospin government, which took power last week after an upset victory in June 1 elections, stunned Bonn and other European partners by saying it wanted a delay to study the so-called stability pact aimed at assuring fiscal discipline after the introduction of the euro.
EU leaders had been due to approve the German-driven pact at a summit in Amsterdam next week but the first statements by France's new administration cast that into doubt.
Jospin's Socialists pledged during the election campaign to redirect European economic policy from austerity towards promoting growth and jobs.
The failure of France's previous centre-right government to keep similar campaign promises was a key reason for its surprise election defeat.

Germany has consistently focused on fiscal discipline and price stability in the run-up to a single currency, but Kohl's reputation was dented when his government proposed revaluing the central bank's gold reserves to qualify for the euro.

European Commission President Jacques Santer said the EU's Dutch presidency had put forward proposals that should pave the way for approval of the stability pact at an EU summit in Amsterdam on Monday and Tuesday.

He told French radio the proposal would integrate a goal to boost employment into plans for more coordination of economic policies under monetary union. But French officials said there would be no numerical target on jobs.

Santer said that if the European Union managed to "give muscle" to two articles in the Maastricht treaty on monetary union -- articles 102a and 103, which provide for economic policy coordination -- "we will certainly have an agreement".
"In the proposal made by the Dutch (EU) presidency, we would also integrate a jobs target in the coordination of economic policy," he said.

German officials said Bonn would not agree to any resolution that gave the European Commission new powers or involved any extra spending on employment measures, nor would it accept any link between the stability pact and an EU statement on growth and jobs.
French officials said they wanted the jobs and growth resolution to be appended to the stability pact.
The summit was widely seen as a test of the close partnership between Bonn and Paris, seen as the dual engines in the drive for European unity.
Financial markets and some European capitals have shown concern that the controversy could undermine the steady march to the euro's launch on January 1, 1999.

Jospin said after talks with European Commission President Jacques Santer on Thursday that progress had been made ahead of the Amsterdam summit towards resolving France's concerns about coordinating economic and employment policy.

Bowing to the EU's new leftward tilt following the British and French elections, Germany agreed this week to add a jobs chapter to the revised Maastricht treaty on European integration which is to come up for ratification in Amsterdam.

Any agreement reached in Poitiers will have to win approval from all 15 EU members. While most are likely to agree to verbal concessions to win France over, some fear Jospin will insist on something more substantive to fulfil his campaign promise.
